title: New Zealand election on a knife edge as National and Labour finish 0.15 points apart
dek: Luxon's coalition is projected to scrape a one-seat majority, but 700,000 special votes are still to be counted and official results are not due until 27 November.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
New Zealand's general election ended without a clear winner on Saturday night, with the ruling National Party and the opposition Labour Party separated by less than a fifth of a percentage point in the preliminary count and about 700,000 special votes still to be counted.

With results in from all voting places, National had 29.37% of the party vote and Labour 29.22%, according to reports. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's governing bloc of National, ACT and New Zealand First was projected to hold 67 of 131 seats, one more than the 66 needed for a majority, but the special votes, which include ballots cast from overseas, could still change the outcome. Official results are due on Friday, 27 November.

## What the leaders said

Mr Luxon said it was "heartening" that National was, on the numbers so far, again the largest party in Parliament, and that "negotiations and compromises are going to be required". He described the result as too close to call.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said "New Zealand has spoken" but that it would take "a little bit longer to figure out" what it had said. "Every vote matters and every vote must now be counted," he said.

## Overhang and kingmakers

New Zealand elects 120 MPs under a mixed-member proportional system, but when a party wins more electorate seats than its share of the party vote would give it, it keeps the extra seats. These "overhang" seats raise the size of Parliament and the number needed for a majority; on the preliminary count the House would have 131 members.

The Opportunity Party, led by Qiulae Wong, crossed the 5% threshold and looks set to enter Parliament for the first time, according to reports, which could make it a kingmaker if the special votes shift the balance. Te Pāti Māori co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer held her Te Tai Hauāuru seat against a Labour challenger in the preliminary count and said her party could work with Opportunity.

## Background

National won the 2023 election with 48 seats and formed a three-party coalition with ACT and New Zealand First, replacing the Labour government. Mr Luxon announced the 7 November election date in January. Under the official timetable, the writ is to be returned and members declared on 3 December, subject to any judicial recounts. One political scientist told reporters that a new government may not be formed before Christmas.

## Why it matters for India

India and New Zealand signed a free trade agreement on 27 April this year, which both governments described as a major step in economic ties. The next government in Wellington will be responsible for carrying the agreement forward, and New Zealand is home to a sizeable Indian community. The two countries' cricket teams are also in the middle of a one-day series in New Zealand, which India lead 2-0.

## What happens next

The Electoral Commission will count the special votes over the coming weeks and declare the official result on 27 November. Coalition talks are likely to begin in earnest only once the final seat numbers are known.
